title: A Systematic Blind-Tasting Method
quiz.0.question: What is the most important reason the SAT blind-tasting system must follow the order S→A→T?
quiz.0.options.0: Alphabetical order is easy to remember
quiz.0.options.1: Smell is the most sensitive sense but tires easily, and alcohol vapour after tasting dulls it
quiz.0.options.2: Visual analysis is the most important step
quiz.0.explanation: Olfactory receptors tire quickly with continued exposure to the same smell (olfactory adaptation), and alcohol vapour after tasting further reduces the ability to identify aromas, so the aroma analysis must be done before tasting.
quiz.1.question: Visual analysis shows "pale garnet + orange rim + high transparency". Which Italian grape does this most likely point to?
quiz.1.options.1: Nebbiolo (low anthocyanins, orange tones even when young)
quiz.1.options.3: Sangiovese (medium red, orange rim only after 5 years)
quiz.1.explanation: Nebbiolo is low in anthocyanins (far lower than Aglianico), mostly of the less stable kinds, so it is naturally pale; as a result, even young wines of 3-5 years show an orange-red rim — the most distinctive visual marker in Italian blind tasting.
quiz.2.question: Aroma analysis finds "rose petal + tar + violet". Which grape is this the core signature of?
quiz.2.options.1: Nebbiolo (rose + tar is its most classic signature combination)
quiz.2.explanation: Nebbiolo contains terpenes (such as geraniol and nerol) associated with its rose aroma; with age, tannins and phenolics polymerise to give tar notes. The two together are Nebbiolo's most classic identifying combination.
quiz.3.question: The palate shows "very high acidity + very high but fine tannins + a 120-second finish". Combined with the pale orange rim and the rose-and-tar nose, what is the deduced conclusion?
quiz.3.options.1: Barolo DOCG, 10-15 years old, possibly a Riserva or single-vineyard MGA
quiz.3.options.2: Aglianico del Vulture (deep purple, does not match the visual)
quiz.3.options.3: Barbaresco (usually softer tannins and less tar)
quiz.3.explanation: Three signatures confirmed together: pale orange rim (S) + rose and tar (A) + very high, fine acid and tannin with a 120-second finish (T) = Nebbiolo. Pronounced tar + very high tannin + a very long finish → Barolo > Barbaresco. Orange rim + tar present → aged 10-15 years.
slides.0.title: A Systematic Blind-Tasting Method
slides.0.subtitle: The three SAT steps: scientific reasoning from observation to deduction
slides.1.title: An Overview of the Three-Step SAT System
slides.1.content:
Blind tasting is a scientific method of analysing wine by the senses alone, free of bias from brand or price. Its core is the three SAT steps, which build a complete chain of evidence, followed by deductive reasoning to reach a conclusion.

👁️ S — SIGHT

30-60 seconds

Depth of colour | hue (purple → orange → brick) | age clues at the rim | transparency | legs as a guide to alcohol

👃 A — AROMA

90-120 seconds

First nose (still) → after swirling | fruit layer | floral layer | spice and oak layer | tertiary aromas of age

👅 T — TASTE

60-90 seconds

Acidity | tannin texture and level | body | alcohol | length and complexity of the finish

🧩 Deductive reasoning

Integrating the SAT data

Identify signature features → form a hypothesis → cross-check → conclude on grape/area/vintage

🟣 Purple rim: young, 0-5 years | the starting point for most Italian grapes
🟠 Orange-red rim: maturing, 8-15 years | the Nebbiolo exception: orange already at 3-5 years
🟤 Brick-brown rim: old wine, 15+ years | anthocyanins largely broken down
⚠️ The Italian trap: pale ≠ light-bodied. Nebbiolo is pale yet high in tannin — the most common misjudgement
slides.3.title: A: Aroma Analysis — Building an Aroma Fingerprint in 90 Seconds
slides.3.content:
Signature Aromas of Three Key Grapes (core identifiers)

🌹 Nebbiolo: rose + tar
Young: violet + rose + red cherry | aged: tar + leather + liquorice + truffle
Why: terpenes (such as geraniol) → rose; high tannins polymerising with age → tar
🍒 Sangiovese: sour cherry + dried herbs
Young: sour cherry + violet + tomato leaf | aged: leather + tobacco + spice
Key: "sour" cherry (not sweet) + dried herbs is the core signature
🫐 Aglianico: black fruit + smoky volcanic notes
Young: blackberry + blackcurrant + liquorice + black pepper | aged: leather + tar + truffle
Character: volcanic soils bring a distinctive smoky minerality; the darkest grape of the South

💡 Nosing technique: first nose (still) → after swirling → identify layer by layer

Once you find a "signature aroma", use secondary features to confirm it, not to overturn it. When "rose + tar" appears → it points strongly to Nebbiolo; then verify with other clues
slides.4.title: T: Palate Analysis + the Four Steps of Deduction
slides.4.content:
The palate provides the final verification data, used to confirm or overturn the aroma hypothesis.

Core Palate Assessments

  • Acidity: high (pH <3.5), a strong reaction at the sides of the tongue → Nebbiolo, Sangiovese, Aglianico
  • Tannin texture: fine and silky vs coarse like sandpaper (an indicator of quality and age)
  • Body: light (Frappato) → full (Amarone)
  • Finish: short = mostly basic wines | medium-long = quality | very long = top wines

The Four Steps of Deduction

  • ① Integrate the SAT data: list every observation and mark 🔥 signature features
  • ② Identify signature features: form initial hypotheses such as "rose and tar → Nebbiolo"
  • ③ Cross-check: see whether all SAT features support the hypothesis; look for contradictions
  • ④ Refine the conclusion: once the grape is confirmed → infer area, age, quality level and price range
Golden rule: every conclusion needs at least 3 independent pieces of SAT evidence. "Rose (A) + pale orange rim (S) + high acid and high tannin (T)" triple-confirmed = Nebbiolo with high confidence
slides.5.title: Key Takeaways
slides.5.points.0: The SAT system: S (sight, 30 s) → A (aroma, 90 s) → T (taste, 60 s) → deduction; the order must not be reversed
slides.5.points.1: Why the order: the sense of smell tires easily (olfactory adaptation), and alcohol vapour after tasting affects smell
slides.5.points.2: Sight: depth of colour indicates the grape family; how orange the rim is indicates age; the Italian trap: pale ≠ light tannin
slides.5.points.3: Nebbiolo's visual signature: pale garnet + orange rim (even when young, at 3-5 years) + high transparency
slides.5.points.4: Nebbiolo's aroma signature: rose + tar (its most classic identifying combination)
slides.5.points.5: Sangiovese's aroma signature: sour cherry + dried herbs (tomato leaf); note "sour", not sweet
slides.5.points.6: Aglianico's aroma signature: black fruit + smoky volcanic notes, with a deep, opaque colour
slides.5.points.7: The four steps of deduction: integrate the data → identify signatures → cross-check → refine the conclusion
slides.5.points.8: Every conclusion needs 3 independent pieces of SAT evidence; blind tasting is deduction, not guessing
slides.6.title: Systematic Blind-Tasting Knowledge Check
slides.6.questions.0.question: What is the most important scientific reason the SAT blind-tasting system must follow the order S→A→T?
slides.6.questions.0.options.0: Alphabetical order is easy to remember
slides.6.questions.0.options.1: Smell tires easily and alcohol vapour after tasting dulls it, so it must be done before tasting
slides.6.questions.0.options.2: Visual analysis is the most important step and must come first
slides.6.questions.0.options.3: It is a rule of the ASI sommelier association
slides.6.questions.0.explanation: Olfactory receptors tire quickly with continued exposure to the same smell (olfactory adaptation); alcohol vapour reaching the nose retronasally after tasting further reduces the ability to identify aromas. So the aroma analysis must be done before tasting.
slides.6.questions.1.question: Visual analysis shows "pale garnet + a clear orange rim + high transparency". Which Italian grape does this most likely point to?
slides.6.questions.1.options.0: Aglianico (deep purple and opaque, purple rim when young)
slides.6.questions.1.options.1: Nebbiolo (low anthocyanins, orange tones even when young at 3-5 years)
slides.6.questions.1.options.3: Sangiovese (medium red, a clear orange rim only after 5 years)
slides.6.questions.1.explanation: Nebbiolo is low in anthocyanins, mostly of the less stable kinds, so it is naturally pale; young wines of 3-5 years already show an orange-red rim — the most distinctive visual marker in Italian blind tasting.
slides.6.questions.2.question: Aroma analysis finds "rose petal + tar + violet". Which grape is this the most classic signature of?
slides.6.questions.2.options.0: Sangiovese (core signature: sour cherry + dried herbs)
slides.6.questions.2.options.1: Nebbiolo (rose + tar is its most classic signature combination)
slides.6.questions.2.options.2: Aglianico (core signature: black fruit + smoky volcanic notes)
slides.6.questions.2.options.3: Barbera (mainly high acid + simple red fruit)
slides.6.questions.2.explanation: Nebbiolo contains terpenes (such as geraniol) associated with its rose aroma; with age, its high tannins polymerise to give tar notes. The two together are Nebbiolo's most classic identifying combination.
slides.6.questions.3.question: In deduction, "pale orange rim (S) + rose and tar (A) + very high, fine acid and tannin + a 120-second finish (T)" leads to which final conclusion?
slides.6.questions.3.options.0: Sangiovese Riserva (gentler tannins, contradicting the very high tannin)
slides.6.questions.3.options.1: Barolo DOCG, 10-15 years old, Riserva or single-vineyard MGA level
slides.6.questions.3.options.2: Aglianico del Vulture (should be deep purple, does not match the visual)
slides.6.questions.3.options.3: Barbaresco DOCG (usually softer tannins and less tar)
slides.6.questions.3.explanation: All three SAT signatures confirm Nebbiolo; pronounced tar + very high tannin + a 120-second finish → Barolo > Barbaresco; orange rim + tar → aged at least 10-15 years.
slides.6.questions.4.question: In SAT blind tasting, what is the most important task of the "T — taste" stage?
slides.6.questions.4.options.1: Providing data on acidity, tannin, body and finish to verify the visual and aroma hypotheses
slides.6.questions.4.options.3: Estimating the price of the wine
slides.6.questions.4.explanation: The core task of the taste stage is "verification": using data on acid intensity, tannin texture and quantity, body and length of finish to confirm or overturn the grape/area hypotheses built in the first two steps.
